reference.python:
import sys

def log2exact(v):
    k = 0
    while v > 1:
        v >>= 1
        k += 1
    return k

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    pos = 0
    cache_bytes = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    assoc = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    block_bytes = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    addr_bits = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    q = int(data[pos]); pos += 1

    sets = cache_bytes // (assoc * block_bytes)
    offset_bits = log2exact(block_bytes)
    index_bits = log2exact(sets)
    tag_bits = addr_bits - offset_bits - index_bits

    out = ["geometry sets %d offsetbits %d indexbits %d tagbits %d"
           % (sets, offset_bits, index_bits, tag_bits)]

    offset_mask = block_bytes - 1
    index_mask = sets - 1
    indices = []

    for _ in range(q):
        a = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
        offset = a & offset_mask
        index = (a >> offset_bits) & index_mask
        tag = a >> (offset_bits + index_bits)
        out.append("%d offset %d index %d tag %d" % (a, offset, index, tag))
        indices.append(index)

    same = sum(1 for i in range(1, len(indices)) if indices[i] == indices[i - 1])
    out.append("sameset %d" % same)
    print("\n".join(out))

main()

explanation:
## The geometry comes first

```cpp
const std::uint64_t sets{ cacheBytes / (assoc * blockBytes) };
const int offsetBits{ log2exact(blockBytes) };
const int indexBits{ log2exact(sets) };
const int tagBits{ addrBits - offsetBits - indexBits };
```

Read the division as a sentence: the cache holds `cacheBytes / blockBytes`
blocks in total, and they are grouped `assoc` to a set, so there are
`cacheBytes / blockBytes / assoc` sets. For the sample: 32768 / 64 = 512 blocks,
8 per set, so 64 sets.

Every one of the three widths is forced by the geometry. Nothing here is a
design choice at decode time - the hardware's wiring picks the bit ranges once,
and this is that wiring written as arithmetic.

## Each field is a shift and a mask

```cpp
offset = a & (blockBytes - 1);
index  = (a >> offsetBits) & (sets - 1);
tag    = a >> (offsetBits + indexBits);
```

The **shift** moves the field down to bit 0; the **mask** cuts off everything
above it. The tag needs no mask because it is the top field - everything above
it is already zero, given that the address fits in `addrBits`.

`blockBytes - 1` works as a mask only because `blockBytes` is a power of two:

```
blockBytes = 64 = 0b1000000
blockBytes - 1  = 0b0111111      exactly offsetBits ones
```

That is the real reason cache sizes, line sizes and page sizes are all powers of
two. `addr % 64` and `addr & 63` are the same value, but the first is a division
circuit and the second is wires - no gates at all for the masked-off bits. When
you see a power of two in hardware, it is usually because somebody wanted a
division to be free.

## Why the offset is at the bottom

```
addresses 0..63 all have the same tag and index, differing only in offset
```

So a whole 64-byte block occupies one cache entry, and reading byte 0 brings
bytes 1 through 63 along with it. That is spatial locality paying off, and it is
why walking an array sequentially costs one miss per 64 bytes instead of one per
element.

Put the offset anywhere else and consecutive bytes would scatter across sets,
making a block meaningless.

## Why the index is in the middle, not at the top

If the index were the **high** bits, then a contiguous region of memory would
map almost entirely into one set, and a program working on a small array would
use a fraction of the cache while evicting itself constantly.

With the index in the middle, consecutive blocks go to consecutive sets and a
sequential walk spreads over the whole cache before coming back round. The hidden
case `0 64 128 192 256` shows it: five consecutive blocks, five different sets,
`sameset 0`.

## How conflicts are built

Two addresses collide when their index matches and their tags differ. The index
repeats every `sets * blockBytes` bytes - the **way size**:

```
way size = sets * blockBytes = 512 * 64 = 32768 bytes = 32 KiB
```

The hidden case `100 132 32868` is exactly this. `100` and `32868` differ by
32768, so they have the same index (1) and different tags (0 and 1) - they
compete for the same set. In a direct-mapped cache those two addresses evict
each other every time, no matter how large the cache is.

That is where the classic power-of-two array stride disaster comes from:

```cpp
double a[1024][1024];
for (int i = 0; i < 1024; ++i) sum += a[i][0];      // stride 8192 bytes
```

Every element of column 0 is 8 KiB apart. With a 32 KiB 8-way L1, 8192 is a
quarter of the way size, so only four distinct sets are ever touched - and the
8 ways in each fill up after 32 rows, after which everything misses. Padding the
row to 1025 doubles breaks the pattern and can make the loop several times
faster without changing a single computation.

`sameset` is in the output for this reason: it is the measurable symptom.

## The degenerate geometries, which are not special cases

**Fully associative**: `sets == 1`, so `indexBits == 0` and the index mask is
`sets - 1 == 0`. Then `(a >> 0) & 0` is `0` for every address - which is right,
because with one set every address is in set 0, and the tag carries the entire
address above the offset. The arithmetic handles it with no `if`.

**Direct-mapped**: `assoc == 1`, so `sets` is the whole block count. Nothing in
the decode changes - associativity only affects how many blocks live in a set,
not how the address is split. Worth noticing: the *fields* depend on `assoc`
only through `sets`.

**`blockBytes == 1`**: `offsetBits == 0`, the offset mask is 0, and every address
is its own block. That is a cache with no spatial locality at all, and it is the
model most textbook examples implicitly use before introducing lines.

Each of these is a hidden case, because an implementation with a special-case
branch usually gets exactly one of them wrong.

## The shift that must not be too large

```cpp
tag = a >> (offsetBits + indexBits);
```

If `offsetBits + indexBits` ever reached 64, this would be **undefined
behaviour** - shifting by the width of the type or more is not "0", it is
unspecified, and on x86 the hardware shift instruction masks the count to 6 bits
so `x >> 64` compiles to `x >> 0` and silently returns `x` unchanged.

Here the statement caps `addrBits` at 48 and the fields must sum to it, so it
cannot happen. In real code that handles arbitrary widths, the guard matters -
and `-fsanitize=undefined` reports it as "shift exponent is too large", which is
one of the clearest sanitizer messages there is.

## Your own machine

```
$ lscpu -C
NAME ONE-SIZE ALL-SIZE WAYS TYPE        LEVEL  SETS
L1d       48K     384K   12 Data            1    64
L1i       32K     256K    8 Instruction     1    64
L2         1M       8M   16 Unified         2  1024
L3        24M      24M   12 Unified         3 16384
```

`SETS`, `WAYS` and the size are exactly the three numbers this problem takes as
input, and `ONE-SIZE / (WAYS * SETS)` gives back the 64-byte line. Worth running,
because the geometry of the machine in front of you is the geometry that decides
whether your loop is fast.
